podcast.title: Comparison to Nobody
podcast.body: The Christian music group "Nobody" is humorously described as "The Shags of Soul," drawing a parallel to their unique style within outsider music. "These are the Shags of Soul."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Critical Acclaim and Influence
podcast.body: The Shags' album *Philosophy of the World* gained legendary status, with notable figures like Frank Zappa praising their work. In 1996, Rolling Stone magazine included the record in its lists of the 100 most influential recordings of the 20th century, one of the greatest garage rock recordings of all time, and one of the 50 most significant indie releases. "Guys like Frank Zappa started singing the praises of the shags."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mention in Outsider Music History
podcast.body: The Shags are listed among artists previously covered as examples of outsider music, alongside Wesley Willis, The Legendary Stardust Cowboy, and others. "On those programs, I covered Wesley Willis, the Shags, the legendary Stardust cowboy, Jandic, Captain B. Fart, Daniel Johnson, Florence Foster Jenkins, and even Charles Manson."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Parental Management and Recording Drive
podcast.body: The band was managed and produced by their father, Austin Wiggins, who, despite being "dirt poor," purchased instruments and arranged lessons for his daughters. He then drove them to Massachusetts, believing them to be at their peak, to record 12 songs in less than a day. "By being dirt poor, he bought his children instruments and paid for lessons. And then he drove everyone down to Massachusetts in order to get his girls on tape while they were at their peak."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Austin Wiggins Era
podcast.body: Following Austin Wiggins' death in 1975, the Wiggins daughters pursued other endeavors, as their father's constant encouragement ceased. However, their album *Philosophy of the World* subsequently achieved legendary, almost mythical status, prompting its rediscovery and critical re-evaluation. "Austin Wiggins died in 1975, and without his constant pushing, the daughters went on to other things."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Worst Group in Recording Studio
podcast.body: The Shags, a trio of sisters from the Woods of New Hampshire, were frequently described as possibly the worst group to ever enter a recording studio. Despite this perception, their material is regarded as the "garageiest" within garage rock and they were name-checked by musicians as far back as the 1970s. "The shags were the three Wiggins sisters. They were managed and produced by their father Austin Wiggins, who for many accounts was just a delusional jerk."

xref.title: Cult Status and Musician Endorsements
xref.body: Despite or because of their unconventional sound, The Shaggs are frequently name-checked by famous musicians who cite their recordings as favorite garage rock albums. They are paradoxically also described as "quite possibly the worst group to ever walk into a recording studio." "The Shags are often named checked by famous musicians, asked to name their favorite garage rock recordings of all time. They are also paradoxically quite possibly the worst group to ever walk into a recording studio."
